strengths: Addresses critical gap in bioimaging ML by systematically investigating what models actually learn; important for foundation model evaluation
Well-designed diagnostic baselines (untrained models, pixel statistics, disentangled tissue structures) provide genuine insight into benchmark behavior

Comprehensive experimental scope across biological scales (cellular/tissue), multiple datasets (RxRx3-core, JUMP-CP, HEST-1k), diverse architectures, with proper cross-validation and statistical reporting
Useful empirical findings showing simple baselines can be competitive, demonstrating how absolute scores mask representation quality issues
Excellent technical rigor with detailed appendices, transparent methodology, synthetic data validation, and reproducibility details
Well-motivated connection to similar benchmarking issues in transcriptomics strengthens field-level implications
Clear, thoughtful presentation with good discussion of limitations
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: findings about untrained network competitiveness are established in computer vision (Ramanujan et al. 2020, Zhong & Andreas 2024); application to bioimaging is useful but somewhat confirmatory

Incomplete causal analysis: when simple baselines succeed, unclear whether due to architectural priors, pixel correlations, or dataset shortcuts; limited diagnostics beyond correlation and representational collapse

Critical results hidden by data availability: MAE-L/8 and MAE-G/8 showing 1.5× improvements on RxRx3-core relegated to Appendix H; this contradicts main narrative that models fail to learn, suggesting bottleneck is dataset size/domain alignment rather than fundamental limitations

Structure-only analysis partially confounded by cell counting: acknowledged but unresolved; synthetic experiments on controlled data may not reflect real tissue complexity; segmentation quality assumed perfect

Dataset-specific choices underexamined: RxRx3-core subsampling to 10 images/gene from highly variable distribution—sensitivity analysis missing; limited explanation for task-dependent learning patterns (why some compounds show learning, others don't)
Vague recommendations: 'need better benchmarks' is main prescription but concrete designs not specified; limited guidance for practitioners on improving models

Overselling of novelty: some claims (e.g., 'surprisingly' competitive baselines) exceed what prior untrained network literature would predict; title frames as critical assessment but findings are mixed—models do learn on some tasks
Experimental fairness issues: hand-crafted cell count features give baselines advantages; PCA+ridge used for structure but different evaluation for image models; not all choices justified

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation across multiple datasets, architectures, and modalities with careful experimental design and detailed protocols enhancing reproducibility

Addresses an important and timely problem: whether bioimaging benchmarks reliably assess what representation learning models actually learn, with well-motivated connection to shortcut learning in related domains
Thoughtfully designed baselines (pixel statistics, untrained models, disentangled tissue structure) that isolate different sources of model performance
Extensive appendices with synthetic validation experiments, multiple pretraining strategies, and detailed analyses demonstrating thoroughness
Clear evidence that some benchmarks can produce misleading conclusions, particularly on cell culture tasks where simple baselines remain competitive
weaknesses: Central claims substantially overstated: models do not uniformly perform 'comparably to baselines'—pretrained ViTs show clear advantages on RxRx3-core (~0.20 vs ~0.15-0.17), and foundation models substantially outperform on HEST-1k tissue imaging (0.37-0.68 vs 0.12-0.34). Dataset-specific results limit generalization claims.

Very limited methodological novelty: untrained baselines extensively studied (Ulyanov et al. 2018; Ramanujan et al. 2020), pixel statistics trivial, tissue structure uses standard segmentation + spatial features. Primarily an empirical audit with no novel solutions beyond vague calls for 'better benchmarks'

Insufficient mechanistic understanding: identifies problems without explaining why they occur or how to address them. Representational collapse discussion (Section 5.2) via PCA is superficial; lacks investigation of which biological signals models do/don't learn

Unresolved confounds in structure-only baseline: strong performance on HEST-1k-1NN likely reflects that gene expression correlates with cell count/density rather than image model failures. While acknowledged (Appendix E.3), this fundamental ambiguity is not convincingly resolved

In-domain results contradict main narrative: H-Optimus-1 shows substantial advantages on tissue benchmarks; OpenPhenom improves on cell culture. These positive findings suggest in-domain models *do* learn useful representations, undermining the negative framing

Statistical rigor issues: no significance testing or multiple comparison corrections; error bars often overlap; no sensitivity analysis for key choices (channel expansion, segmentation source, RxRx3-core subsampling to 10 images per gene)
Limited practical guidance: unclear what practitioners should do with findings. Should foundation models be avoided? Used only in-domain? No actionable recommendations provided

Dataset-specific findings with unclear generalization: only two biological scales examined; findings may not transfer to other imaging modalities or biological tasks; synthetic experiments use simplified patterns

strengths: Addresses critical gap: systematic investigation of what representation learning models actually learn in microscopy, with timely relevance to foundation model evaluation

Comprehensive experimental design: multiple datasets (RxRx3-core, JUMP-CP, HEST-1k), diverse architectures, natural image reference for comparison, proper statistical handling with multiple folds and seeds

Well-motivated baseline construction: untrained models cleanly separate architectural priors from learned biology; pixel statistics provide intuitive bounds; disentangled tissue structure (cell graphs) is clever and enables morphology vs. organization dissection

Important empirical findings: RxRx3-core shows untrained ViTs competitive with pretrained models; pixel statistics recover substantial signal; layer-wise analysis reveals different patterns than natural images, challenging assumptions about model capabilities

Methodological rigor: honest treatment of confounds (e.g., cell count effects), synthetic validation experiments, multiple evaluation perspectives (correlations, gene-wise, dimensionality), transparent acknowledgment of limitations
Practical impact: provides diagnostic framework for benchmarking with clear relevance to growing bioimage analysis field; parallels important concerns in transcriptomics
Strong reproducibility: public datasets, detailed configurations, extensive appendices with implementation details
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: baseline concepts (untrained networks, pixel statistics, structure extraction) individually sensible but not conceptually novel; contribution is systematic application rather than new techniques

Incomplete causal analysis in tissue imaging: does not definitively establish whether structure-only models learn spatial organization vs. primarily capture cell count; proposed matching and intervention analyses not fully executed; synthetic experiments helpful but on artificial data

Limited analysis of why failures occur: establishes that models don't learn expected features but offers incomplete insight into causes (benchmark shortcuts? dataset artifacts? architecture limitations? task formulation?); deeper failure mode analysis would strengthen claims

Representational dimensionality analysis is correlational: Figure 16 shows correlation between PCA variance and performance but not causation; limited interpretation of what collapse means mechanistically

Incomplete evaluation of strong in-domain models: MAE-L/8 and MAE-G/8 show 1.5× improvements but proprietary weights prevent layer-wise analysis; creates gap where best-performing models are inaccessible for detailed investigation

Limited scope and generalization: findings specific to Cell Painting and H&E histology; unclear generalization to other staining, modalities, tissues, or clinical settings; diagnostic for specific benchmarks rather than prescriptive for field broadly

Statistical rigor could be stronger: differences sometimes small relative to variability; lacks formal significance testing and confidence intervals for correlations; could benefit from bootstrap comparisons

Limited constructive guidance: convincingly diagnoses problems but incompletely specifies solutions; 'more diagnostic benchmarks' identified but not detailed; limited concrete recommendations for robustness testing

strengths: Addresses critical and timely problem of what deep learning models actually learn in microscopy imaging, mirroring important findings in transcriptomics
Comprehensive experimental scope spanning multiple organizational scales, datasets (RxRx3-core, JUMP-CP, HEST-1k, BRACS, BACH), and models (foundation models, CNNs, ViTs, untrained networks)
Well-designed baseline strategies: pixel statistics, untrained encoders, and novel disentangled tissue structure representations that isolate different information sources
Rigorous multi-faceted analysis including layer-wise evolution, dimensionality analysis via PCA, ranking correlations, per-compound/gene breakdowns, and controlled synthetic experiments
Clear and consistent demonstration that simple baselines are unexpectedly competitive across diverse tasks, challenging assumptions about benchmark validity
Strong reproducibility: public code promised, all data/models public, extensive implementation details in appendices
Provides actionable recommendations for improved benchmarking practices (reporting baselines, layer-wise curves, diagnostic breakdowns)
weaknesses: Causal claims about shortcuts are primarily inferred from correlation rather than direct evidence; that untrained and pretrained ViTs have correlated rankings could indicate both capture validly informative features rather than proving both exploit only low-level signals

Structure-only baseline substantially confounded by cell count, particularly on COAD/PRAD datasets; while acknowledged in appendix, this undermines claims about structure as independent modality and is underemphasized in main text

Strong conclusions significantly tempered by success of in-domain models (MAE-L/8, MAE-G/8 achieve 1.5× higher recall, H-Optimus-1 shows clear depth-dependent improvements); suggests problems may be training-data-related rather than fundamental benchmark flaws

Limited investigation of root causes: paper demonstrates what fails but provides insufficient insight into why (dataset biases? insufficient signal? architectural misalignment?); root cause analysis would enable targeted solutions beyond generic recommendations

Lacks biological validation: no demonstration that high benchmark performance correlates with downstream utility or biological insights; doesn't address whether models exploit artifacts or discover meaningful biology
Methodological choices lack full justification: RxRx3-core subsampling to 10 images per gene (from ~50-9,450), adjusted similarity thresholds, and sensitivity to these choices unexplored
Limited cross-dataset generalization analysis; mostly in-domain evaluations underexplore OOD transfer critical for foundation model validation

Presentation issues: 45-page manuscript is dense with key results scattered across appendices; important limitations (cell-count confounds) underemphasized in main text; generic design principles in Section 5.3 ('report baselines') lack specificity
